Vitamin C has also been proposed for prevention of malignancy but there is no real evidence to justify it. It certainly appears to be ineffective as adjuvant therapy in the treatment of advanced ma- lignancy,28 and combination with betacarotene and vitamin E failed to show any effect in preventing colorectal adenoma.15 At physiological concentrations vitamin C is an important antoxi- dant,3 but while low serum ascorbic acid concentrations have been inversely related to cancer mortality,29,30 supplementation is unlikely to be justified in anyone eating a balanced diet.1 There is epidemiological evidence that vitamin D has protective effects against the development of malignant neoplasms,31 but evidence from controlled studies is scanty, and it is unclear whether supplementation, and if so to what degree, would be ap- propriate. Vitamin E substances are also known to play an important an- toxidant role in the body. Animal studies have suggested that they should inhibit tumour production, and the Chinese study men- tioned above found combined antoxidant therapy including vita- min E to be of benefit in the primary prevention of stomach and oesophageal cancers.16 Other studies in western populations have generally been disappointing; vitamin E had no effect on lung cancer incidence in those at risk,17,18 and did not prevent the development of new colorectal adenomas.15 In a study of pa- tients with head and neck cancer, supplementation with vitamin E led to a higher incidence of second primary cancers and re- duced cancer-free survival; patients on supplements had initially also been given betacarotene. While noting the fact that the study population were at high-risk for second primary cancers, the authors cautioned against the use of high-dose vitamin E supple- ments for cancer prevention.32 There is also suggestion of in- creased all-cause mortality with high-dose vitamin E (see p.1993). However, further analysis of the lung-cancer study33 suggests that vitamin E may have protected against prostate can- cer. There is preliminary evidence that selenium (see p.1961) or vitamin E supplementation may reduce the risk of prostate can- cer, and a large randomised study is underway to further investi- gate this. Results from the Nurses’ Health Study have indicated that pro- longed use of multivitamins was associated with reduced risk of developing cancer of the colon.34 This effect was thought to be due to the folate component and could be demonstrated after 15 years of use, but not after shorter-term ingestion. Dietary folate was also associated with a modest reduction in risk for colon can- cer, and folic acid intake might reduce the risk of breast cancer, especially in those regularly consuming alcohol.35,36 For the sug- gestion that folic acid may have dual modulatory effects on car- cinogenesis, see Carcinogenicity, under Folic Acid, p.1940
